item.title: Holga Afternoon: a celebration of the imperfect camera
item.description:
The Holga is a plastic medium format camera that doesn’t focus, doesn’t meter the light and forgives no mistake. And that is precisely why it is one of the best loved cameras in analogue photography.

Every year, from 1 to 7 October, photographers all over the world take to the streets with the same camera to celebrate Holga Week. We celebrate it the next day, on Thursday 8 October, with a free afternoon at Nau Bostik.

item.title: A year on the street. Twelve photographers. A book of your own.
item.description:
Street photography is not learned in a weekend workshop. It is learned on the street, with time, with mistakes and with a lot of patience. But you learn it far better if you have a frame: references to argue with, a group to share the process with, and someone who reads your work and asks you uncomfortable questions.

From Street to Book is Llumàtics’ annual course in analogue street photography. Twelve monthly sessions, each devoted to a photographer or a foundational movement of the genre. Joan Colom and Català-Roca to start at home. Cartier-Bresson, Robert Frank, Winogrand, Diane Arbus, Saul Leiter, Koudelka, Moriyama, Alex Webb and Martin Parr to widen the gaze. Every session is a different universe. Every session asks the same question: how would you do it?

item.title: Making a real photobook. From scratch.
item.description:
Having images is the starting point. Turning them into a book is a completely different decision. A photobook forces you to choose — which images go in, which do not, in what order, in whose voice — and every decision defines what the whole thing is about.

The new Photobook: from concept to object workshop is for those who want to take that step seriously. It is not a Photoshop course or a printing tutorial: it is complete guidance from the concept to the file ready for the printer.

item.title: Positivador WebApp, a small tool to help us in the darkroom
item.description:
In the courses we teach, students —and teachers too— have always struggled to interpret a negative image correctly. After making a direct paper negative portrait, or when looking at freshly developed film, it’s perfectly normal for our brains to have difficulty reading a negative as the image it will become once printed.

Not sure if it’s overdeveloped or underdeveloped? Still finding it hard to read shadow densities? Don’t worry! You can now download for free the Positivador web app, which we designed and developed together with LinuxBCN to make it easy to visualise the positive image directly on your phone. You can also flip it horizontally —the negative is mirrored, after all—, rotate the image, freeze the frame and —in the pro version— save it to your device.

item.title: First development: when the negative appears
item.description:
We ran the first film developing workshop. Not the first I’ve ever done, but the first here, in the new space.

The mechanics are the same as always: mix the chemicals, load the reel in total darkness, develop with care and wash with patience. But the reaction when someone opens the tank and sees the negative for the first time — that look of surprise mixed with “of course, it was always going to work” — never gets old.

item.title: Large Format Portraits — An analogue experience for everyone
item.description:
There was a moment in the workshop, while we were developing the first portrait on paper, when someone said: “Wait — you can actually see the face.” Yes. The face of the person standing in front of you, appearing in black and white inside a tray. It’s wonderful the first time. The fifth time too.

How it went

At Cameras & Films we brought our large format camera — the Woody, an old 4×5" wooden camera — and spent the morning making portraits. The setup: part of the group posed, the other part photographed, and we rotated.

item.title: Caffenol: developing with coffee
item.description:
Caffenol is one of the best-known recipes in alternative development. The name comes from caffeine + phenol, the active components that make coffee develop silver. Ascorbic acid (vitamin C) acts as an accelerator. Sodium carbonate regulates the pH. Together, a solution that genuinely works.

Why it’s worth knowing

It’s not a trick. Caffenol produces negatives you can print, scan and work with. The results have their own character: a certain softness in the grain, a tonal response slightly different from conventional developers. Not better or worse. Just different.

item.title: Cameraless cyanotype prints at Nau Bostik
item.description:
On 15 November we ran the free cameraless cyanotype workshop at Nau Bostik. Fifteen places. Fifteen people. None of them had ever made a cyanotype before.

The formula is simple: two iron salts, paper and sunlight. But “simple” doesn’t mean “no surprises”. Every sheet of paper responds differently. November light in Barcelona is not the same as August light. And the objects people bring — leaves, feathers, keys, a magnifying glass, a phone negative printed onto an acetate at the last minute — completely change the result.

item.title: World Pinhole Photography Day 2025
item.description:
On 27 April we are celebrating World Pinhole Photography Day at the Sala Basiana of the Nau Bostik.

The proposal is simple: come, experiment and take photographs with no more structure than each person wants to give it. The AWPCP.org association lends cameras to anyone who does not have one. Some of the results will be developed in the Llumàtics lab.

No plans, no rules and, above all, no lenses.

item.title: A day of analogue development: rain, Zenit cameras and a real passion for photography
item.description:
On 2 February we ran the introduction to development workshop at Cameras & Films (the former Lomography Embassy Barcelona). It was raining.

The students headed out into the streets of the Born with Zenit cameras fitted with Helios lenses and Fomapan 100. Because the light was poor, we pushed it to ISO 800. Twenty minutes on the street, then back to the lab.

From there on: loading the spiral, mixing the chemistry, developing. Ninety minutes of the complete process.

item.title: Rain, Zenits and a serious passion for analogue photography
item.description:
On 1 February, at Cameras & Films (formerly Lomography Store Barcelona), we ran one of our most beloved workshops: film developing in black and white.

Despite the day starting with a few hiccups, it ended up being a rich, rewarding experience.

The day

Rain arrived from the morning, which forced us to rethink some parts of the workshop on the fly. Light was in short supply, and I myself — yes, a little unprepared — hadn’t come ready enough for such a wet day.

item.title: Large Format Portraits at Cameras & Films — August 2024
item.description:
Bring Arezzo — said the workshop announcement — and come learn to load, focus and shoot our old large format Woody camera.

The idea: we combine the experience of operating a large format camera with portrait technique. You arrive as a photographer and leave having also been a model. Or the other way round.

Best of all: we developed the portraits immediately in the shop’s darkroom. All the magic of analogue photography, live.

item.title: Developing workshop at Cameras & Films — July 2024
item.description:
Another black-and-white developing workshop at Cameras & Films (formerly Lomography Embassy Barcelona).

Learning to develop a roll of film is one of those things that, once you’ve done it, you can’t stop. Loading the film into the tank in the dark, measuring the chemicals, checking the temperature, agitating, waiting. And when you open the tank and see there’s an image… there’s nothing quite like it.

item.title: Push processing at the Barcelona Blues Festival
item.description:
Two sessions. First the concert, then the darkroom.

Friday night we went to the Barcelona Blues Festival. 35mm rolls loaded at ISO 3200 (3-stop push). Low light, lots of grain, loads of adrenaline. Vanessa Collier on stage and us in the front row with the Leicas.

Sunday morning we came in to develop. We applied everything we’d learnt on Saturday about push development: extending the development time to compensate for the underexposure and bring back the shadows. The result: dense negatives, high contrast, expressive grain. Exactly what we were after.

item.title: Open days at the Nau Bostik
item.description:
On 26 November the Nau Bostik opened its doors. Llumàtics took part with a small exhibition of large format portraits and a simple offer: anyone who wanted one got a portrait taken.

Vintage large format camera, a Sunday morning and a lot of film.

item.title: Halloween 2020 — Bodypaint and analogue photography
item.description:
For Halloween 2020 we combined two things we like: body painting and analogue photography.

Four session options — face or body painting, for one or two people — each with 30 minutes of analogue photographic session included. The sessions took place at the Nau Bostik.

See the photographs →

item.title: Registration open for one-to-one sessions
item.description:
Would you like a 100% analogue one-to-one session? Get in touch and we will arrange a session tailored to you.

As well as the digitised results, we offer paper prints at whatever size you want. Write to us and let’s talk it over.

item.title: Llumàtics moves to the Nau Bostik
item.description:
After three years in the Poble Sec, Llumàtics is moving to a new location.

In a few weeks we expect to have the new premises ready to resume our usual activity: chemical photography, the real thing, inside the Nau Bostik. There, surrounded by a setting and rooms that are second to none, we will go on offering training, large format sessions and a few surprises we are preparing.

item.title: La Fiesta Pinholera Perversa at Nau Bostik
item.description:
The day started at 10:00 in the morning, with Nau Bostik open to everyone.

At La Perversa we held an open day: the darkroom accessible, the studio available, and if you brought your camera and photographic paper, you could develop your own photos from the day. No fuss. Those who wanted to learn, learnt. Those who wanted to watch, watched.

The experimental pinhole workshop was led by Alfonso de Castro with Santi Pladellorens from Analogueworks, who brought along some of his cameras in very different formats for participants to use. Fifteen euros, limited places, and one of the best sessions of the year.

item.title: Dr. Roland F. Beers' Paper Developer: a paper developer with contrast control
item.description:
Laboratory and more laboratory. Luckily, I love it.

I had wanted for some time to play “Breaking Bad” in the Llumàtics lab. And I had had the Formulas de Digital Truth app on my phone for a while — a good collection of chemical formulas for making developers, fixers and many other brews, experimental or not, for photography.

Thanks to Alfonso de Castro’s recommendations I focused on the Dr. Roland F. Beers’ Paper Developer. Why this one? Very simple: I could buy all the components in Barcelona and, by mixing parts A and B in different proportions, get developers with varying degrees of contrast. One developer, seven possible contrasts.

item.title: Guinneol: developing a roll with Guinness beer
item.description:
I always try out new development systems. The more experimental the better — it is the best way to keep the workshops fresh and to really understand what happens inside the tank.

This time: Guinness beer.

The recipe I found was called “Guinnes” and the translation was, let’s say, creative — it talked about “detergent” when it clearly meant soda carbonate. It is not the first time a bad translation complicates a process that should be simple. But with a bit of chemical judgement, it sorts itself out.
